content: Tsuga, commonly known as hemlock, is a genus of coniferous trees within the family Pinaceae. The name hemlock originates from the similarity in the smell of crushed foliage to that of the unrelated herb poison hemlock. However, unlike the herb, Tsuga species are not toxic. The genus comprises between eight and ten species, depending on the taxonomic authority, with four species native to North America and four to six species found in eastern Asia. Tsuga trees are medium to large evergreen trees, typically ranging in height from 20 to 60 meters, with some species reaching up to 79 meters. They exhibit a conical to irregular crown, with the latter form more common in certain Asian species. The leading shoots of these trees often droop. Their bark is scaly and deeply furrowed, varying in color from gray to brown. The branches extend horizontally from the trunk and are usually arranged in flattened sprays that bend downward at their tips. Short spur shoots, common in many gymnosperms, are weakly to moderately developed in Tsuga. The young twigs and distal portions of the stems are flexible and often pendulous. The stems are rough due to persistent pulvini left behind after leaf fall. Winter buds are ovoid or globose, rounded at the apex, and non-resinous. The leaves of Tsuga are flattened to slightly angular, measuring 5–35 mm in length and 1–3 mm in width. They are borne singly and arranged spirally on the stem, with their bases twisted so that the leaves lie flat on either side of the stem or, less commonly, radiate outward. Toward the base, the leaves narrow abruptly into a petiole, which is set on a forward-angled pulvinus. The petiole is twisted at its base, aligning almost parallel to the stem. The leaf apex may be notched, rounded, or acute. The undersides of the leaves feature two white stomatal bands separated by an elevated midvein, though these bands are inconspicuous in T. mertensiana. The upper leaf surface lacks stomata, except in T. mertensiana. Each leaf contains a single resin canal located beneath the vascular bundle. The pollen cones of Tsuga grow solitarily from lateral buds. They are 3–5 mm long (occasionally up to 10 mm), ovoid, globose, or ellipsoid, and range in color from yellowish-white to pale purple. These cones are borne on short peduncles. The pollen itself has a sac-like, ring-shaped structure at its distal pole, which is occasionally doubly sac-like. The seed cones are borne on year-old twigs and are small, ovoid-globose, or oblong-cylindric, measuring 15–40 mm in length, except in T. mertensiana, where they are cylindrical and longer, ranging from 35–80 mm. These cones are solitary, terminal, or rarely lateral, pendulous, and either sessile or borne on short peduncles up to 4 mm long. The cones mature within 5–8 months, and the seeds are shed shortly thereafter. The cones themselves are shed soon after seed release or up to a year or two later. The seed scales are thin, leathery, and persistent, varying in shape and lacking an apophysis or umbo. The bracts are small and included within the cone. The seeds are small, measuring 2–4 mm in length, and are winged, with the wing measuring 8–12 mm. They also contain small adaxial resin vesicles. Seed germination is epigeal, and the seedlings typically have four to six cotyledons. The mountain hemlock (T. mertensiana) is unique within the genus due to several characteristics. Its leaves are less flattened and arranged all around the shoot, with stomata present on both the upper and lower surfaces, giving the foliage a glaucous appearance. Additionally, its cones are the longest in the genus, measuring 35–80 mm in length and cylindrical rather than ovoid. Some botanists classify it in a distinct genus, Hesperopeuce mertensiana, though it is more commonly treated as a subgenus. Another species, the bristlecone hemlock, initially described as Tsuga longibracteata, is now placed in a separate genus, Nothotsuga. This species differs from Tsuga in having erect (not pendulous) cones with exserted bracts and male cones clustered in umbels, features that align it more closely with the genus Keteleeria. Tsuga species are adapted to moist, cool temperate regions with high rainfall, cool summers, and minimal water stress. They are also well-suited to environments with heavy winter snowfall and are more tolerant of ice storms than most other tree species. The eastern North American species, T. canadensis and T. caroliniana, face significant threats from the sap-sucking insect Adelges tsugae (hemlock woolly adelgid). This pest, related to aphids, was accidentally introduced from eastern Asia, where it is a minor pest. Extensive mortality has occurred, particularly east of the Appalachian Mountains. Asian Tsuga species are resistant to this pest, while the two western American hemlocks exhibit moderate resistance. Tsuga species also serve as food plants for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, including the autumnal moth and the engrailed moth, as well as older caterpillars of the gypsy moth. The foliage of young trees is often browsed by deer, and the seeds are consumed by finches and small rodents. Older trees are frequently attacked by fungal pathogens such as Heterobasidion annosum and Armillaria species, which cause heartwood decay and increase susceptibility to windthrow. Rhizina undulata can kill groups of trees following minor grass fires that activate the growth of its spores. The wood of hemlocks is valuable in the timber industry, particularly for wood pulp production. Many Tsuga species are also cultivated for horticultural purposes, with numerous cultivars selected for use in gardens.
